items.what: Shopping.lua TrainingSteps (304-320) re-derives the order of training steps by sorting ranks at rank.reqSkill and recipes at atSkill - modifier, while ns.RouteSteps (Route.lua:167-190) is the canonical walk used by the route page and by the public API (API.lua:181, consumed by Adventure Guide Forever): ranks once a segment passes cap - 75, a recipe's training just before its first craft. The tracker's 'next thing to train' (and the trainer it waypoints to, which depends on steps[1].cap) therefore disagrees with the page and the API. The trainer-cap rule 'reqSkill + 1' is also restated at Shopping.lua:313 and API.lua:190.
items.why: In-memory LuaJIT repro (/tmp/shoprepro/order.lua) loads Locales/enUS.lua, Route.lua and Shopping.lua with stubbed host APIs; profession Tailoring base 40, route.ranks = {Journeyman cap 150 reqSkill 50}, route.training = {recipe 7 at 60}, segments 60->75 (recipe 7) and 75->100 (recipe 8). Tracker first objective: 'Train Journeyman at 50 (+1 more)'. ns.RouteSteps order: train recipe 7, craft, rank Journeyman, craft. So the tracker tells the player to train Journeyman first and would pick a trainer teaching up to 150, while the page/API say train recipe 7 first (trainer cap 61). The Shopping comment ('ranks when the trainer allows them') and Route comment ('each rank once the route passes the cap below it') state different rules for the same concept; one should be canonical (derive the tracker's steps from ns.RouteSteps, taking the first rank/training walk entry).
items.reason: The tracker's TrainingSteps walks ns.RouteSteps, the route page's order
items.guard: lens-only: a behaviour bug, not a shape a rule can match; regression test tests/shopping_spec.lua 'the same training'

items.quote:
function ns.SetTracked(skillLine, tracked)
	ns.db.trackedProfessions[skillLine] = tracked or nil
	PlaySound(tracked and SOUNDKIT.IG_MAINMENU_OPTION_CHECKBOX_ON or SOUNDKIT.IG_MAINMENU_OPTION_CHECKBOX_OFF)
	ns.RefreshTracker()
end
items.what: Tracking or untracking a profession leaves the public API's cached profession order stale.
items.why: Behaviour bug found while tracing the trackedProfessions write and its readers, not a deletion candidate. API.lua Build sorts by ns.IsTracked, but API.Professions returns its cached table until invalidated. SetTracked only plays a sound and calls RefreshTracker; that marks the tracker dirty and refreshes the merchant button without invalidating the API. Repository-wide searches for trackedProfessions and InvalidateAPI, plus inspection of the Route.lua Track callback, Shopping.lua Stop tracking callback, and API.lua event handler, found no invalidation on this mutation. An in-memory LuaJIT reproduction loaded the actual Model.lua, Shopping.lua and API.lua with host stubs, two capped professions and empty routes. API.Professions initially returned Alchemy first. After the actual ns.SetTracked(197, true), ns.IsTracked(197) was true but API.Professions returned the same table with Alchemy first. Explicit ns.InvalidateAPI() immediately put Tailoring first. Untracking reproduced the inverse stale order. Thus external API consumers miss the tracking priority change until an unrelated invalidating event. Invalidate the API when tracking changes.
items.reason: SetTracked calls ns.InvalidateAPI
items.guard: lens-only: a behaviour bug, not a shape a rule can match; regression test tests/api_spec.lua 'tracking a profession rebuilds the list'

items.quote: buyButton:SetScript("OnClick", BuyMissing)
items.what: The 'Buy tracked reagents' button stays enabled after a click; BuyMissing recomputes what is missing from C_Item.GetItemCount, which only changes when the server's bag update arrives. A second click before BAG_UPDATE_DELAYED/MERCHANT_UPDATE refreshes buys every missing reagent again, silently spending gold on a duplicate order.
items.why: BuyMissing (174-190) calls MerchantPurchases each click; nothing records in-flight purchases, disables or hides buyButton until RefreshBuyButton runs from an event (431). Not reproducible headless (depends on server latency); needs a /reload test: at a vendor with a large missing order, double-click the button and compare bag counts. Money path, so worth disabling the button in BuyMissing until the next refresh.
items.reason: Two successive unchanged BuyMissing calls with unchanged bag counts submit 20 units for a 10-unit rounded order, but that harness does not establish when the live client updates GetItemCount or disables merchant interactions. A Forever vendor capture of rapid repeated clicks and bag/merchant event timing is required to prove actual duplicate spending.

items.quote: local stack = math.max(info.stackCount or 1, 1)
items.what: A missing or nonpositive merchant stackCount is silently replaced with one, inventing the unit basis for the displayed cost and automatic purchase quantities.
items.why: MerchantPurchases accepts an item record with a positive price without validating its stackCount, then uses the substituted one to round purchase units and divide the stack price. RefreshBuyButton displays that cost and BuyMissing uses those quantities and the cost for its affordability check. Repository-wide searches found the same fallback in Prices.lua but no documented contract making one the correct substitute for unavailable stack data. An in-memory LuaJIT reproduction invoked the unchanged MerchantPurchases with seven missing units and a price of 100: nil, zero and negative stackCount each yielded stack=1, count=7 and cost=700; a stackCount of five yielded count=10 and cost=200. The invalid inputs were synthetic, so this demonstrates the fallback and its downstream effect, not that the client currently emits these records. Under the project convention, unknown quantity data should remain unknown rather than become a plausible purchase.
items.reason: The pinned MerchantItemInfo contract allows missing stackCount and defaults it to 0 without guaranteeing a positive price implies a positive quantity; Shopping substitutes one, unlike Prices' validated merchant observer. The unchanged-path probe calculates count=7/cost=700 for nil, zero or negative stack versus count=10/cost=200 for stack=5, proving invented purchase and affordability quantities for allowed incomplete data.

items.what: Suggestion kind is a closed set of five magic numbers: Kind() returns 1..5 (Sources.lua:214-225), KIND_TEXT is positionally indexed (238), ns.SuggestionNPC tests `suggestion.kind <= 2` to mean 'a vendor' (232), and RecipeSuggestions sorts on the number (273-274); types/Namespace.lua types it as plain `integer`.

The closed-set finding survives, and introducing named kinds is a design choice. items.quote:
local function Band(t, skill)
	if skill < t[1] then
		return string.format(L["needs %d"], t[1]), ns.COLORS.red
	end
	for i, band in ipairs(BAND_NAMES) do
		if skill < t[i + 1] then
			return string.format(L["%s until %d"], BAND_LABELS[band], t[i + 1]), ns.COLORS[band]
		end
	end
	return L["grey"], ns.COLORS.grey
end
items.what: Tooltip.lua:280-290 (Band) independently implements the difficulty classification in Model.lua:16-33 (Model.Color). Model is the canonical home for choosing the band; Tooltip should only format its label and ending threshold.
items.why: Repository-wide searches for Model.Color, BAND_NAMES, BAND_LABELS and threshold comparisons show that Core.Describe delegates classification to Model.Color, while item tooltips reach this second classifier through AttachItemTooltips -> AddUses -> AddUsedIn -> Band. Model uses explicit comparisons; Band uses a separate ordered colour list and repeats the red and grey cases. An in-memory LuaJIT comparison of the actual functions matched all 204 cases across ordinary thresholds, equal orange/yellow thresholds, equal yellow/green thresholds and fully collapsed bands. There is no current classification drift, but any correction to band boundaries must be applied twice. Band additionally returns localized text and the next threshold; those presentation differences are intentional and must be preserved. Model accepts nil thresholds, while Uses already filters them out before Band runs. Route.lua:265-284 displays all learnable bands rather than classifying the current skill, so its distinct presentation is not another copy of this classifier.
items.guard: lens-only: two classifiers written differently (a loop versus explicit comparisons) need judgment to match

items.quote: local BAND_LABELS = { orange = L["orange"], yellow = L["yellow"], green = L["green"] }
items.what: The colour-band name list and label map are restated: Tooltip.lua:39 (`{ "orange", "yellow", "green", "grey" }`) and :272 BAND_LABELS, and Route.lua:293-294 BAND_NAMES/BAND_LABELS. Canonical home would be one shared table beside ns.COLORS (Core.lua:51) or Model.Color's bands.
items.why: Tooltip's copy has drifted (no grey label; grey handled by a separate branch in Band()), Route's has all four. A renamed or added band needs edits in three places; ns.COLORS and Model.Color hold the same closed set.
items.reason: The displayed labels are selected from the same Model.Color domain, with Tooltip's terminal grey branch deliberately separate; the repeated closed band set is already retained at its source, same producer as 9ffd581251. It is not an independent current tooltip/route rendering bug.

Hover one for what your other characters hold ([Syndicator](https://www.curseforge.com/wow/addons/syndicator), same realm and faction), and with *Reagents you gather are free* on (the default) anything another of your professions gathers (Light Leather with Skinning, ore with Mining, herbs with Herbalism) costs nothing, so the route can use it, and it's listed as *gather*. *Track* puts it in the objective tracker above your quests, like `12/20 Linen Cloth`, kept up to date as you buy, craft and skill up; click the training line or a vendor reagent's line for a waypoint to the nearest trainer or vendor, and hover it to see who and where. items.quote: a map tab under the Professions window's side tabs opens a SkillUp page. Pick any of your professions (it starts on the open one) and type a target skill: the page lists the cheapest crafts, like `12× Heavy Linen Bandage to 90`, each with its cost, then the total. Each skill point takes the recipe with the lowest cost per skill-up at that point. Recipes a trainer teaches are included when they pay for themselves, fee counted once and never before the trainer would teach them, shown as a *Train* step with its fee. Steps are a table of recipe, crafts, target skill and cost; hover one for the crafted item, its colour bands, the reagents for that step and its cost, or click it to open the recipe. *Craft* under the route crafts its first step as many times as it needs and your bags allow, while that profession is open. Reagents show where each price comes from and how old it is, and the page flags auction prices older than a day. Auction prices need [Auctionator](https://www.curseforge.com/wow/addons/auctionator); without it, a reagent sold only at the auction house has no price. The target can go past your current cap, up to the last rank a trainer teaches: the route then adds *Train Journeyman/Expert/Artisan* steps with the fee, the skill the trainer wants and, while you are below it, the level. Fees come from the classic trainer data (CMaNGOS) until you visit a trainer, whose own fees then win. Recipes with an unpriced reagent are left out and counted, and if nothing you know skills up far enough the route stops there and says so, then lists the recipes from vendors, quests and drops that would carry it on: easiest to get first (a vendor of your faction, then limited supply, quests, named drops, world drops), with the scroll's price and how far each reaches. Hover one for every vendor, quest and drop with its zone and coordinates; click it for a waypoint to the nearest vendor or the likeliest drop ([Shortest Path Forever](https://www.curseforge.com/wow/addons/shortest-path-forever)'s travel route when installed, else [TomTom](https://www.curseforge.com/wow/addons/tomtom)'s arrow, else the map's own). *Train* steps and vendor reagents name the nearest trainer (one who teaches that far, of your faction) or vendor with its zone and coordinates (the quickest to reach by Shortest Path Forever's travel time when it is installed), and a click sets a waypoint there.
items.what: 'Fees come from the classic trainer data (CMaNGOS) until you visit a trainer, whose own fees then win.' sits in the sentence run about the Train Journeyman/Expert/Artisan rank steps, but rank fees never use a visited trainer's fee.
items.why: Route.lua NextRanks builds rank fees only from ns.TrainerRanks (generated by tools/gen_trainer.py); ns.db.trainer (written in Trainer.lua) is read only by ns.TrainingFor for recipe services. So the seen-fee override applies to Train <recipe> steps, not rank steps. Also 'Pick any of your professions' is inaccurate: ns.RouteProfessions drops GATHERING (Herbalism, Fishing, Skinning), so those never appear in the dropdown.

items.what: The ordering checks cannot fail on the sort keys they name. Blacksmithing (craft first) vs Leatherworking (buy first) are both untracked with steps, and "Blacksmithing" < "Leatherworking" alphabetically, so API.lua's final `a.name < b.name` tiebreak yields the same order without the Urgency(entry) key. The comment also states the precedence as 'Tracked first', while API.lua:285-287 sorts 'something to do first, then tracked'; no fixture distinguishes the two.
items.why: Proved in a scratch copy: deleting `Urgency(entry)` from `urgency[entry]` in API.lua:285 -> `api_spec: 79 checks passed`; swapping the first two keys (tracked before has-steps) -> also 79 passed. The KIND_ORDER/Urgency ranking and the has-steps-over-tracked precedence are untested. Fix: rename a fixture so the name tiebreak disagrees with the intended order (e.g. give the buy-first profession a name sorting before the craft-first one, and add a tracked profession with no steps), and correct the comment to the production order.
items.reason: Reversing KIND_ORDER's craft and buy priorities fails the craft-before-shopping assertion, so the check can fail; surviving mutations show a coverage gap, not an inert test

items.quote: if hashlib.sha256(path.read_bytes()).hexdigest() != expected:
items.what: Freshly downloaded data is written and then read back and hashed again
items.why: The download branch already compared the same bytes to `expected` two lines earlier; only the cached path needs the second check, so restructure as download-if-missing then a single verify of path.read_bytes(), or verify in the else
items.reason: The first checksum validates downloaded bytes before acceptance, while the read-back checksum validates the cache file actually handed to the native integration harness and also catches pre-existing corrupt cache content. These are distinct network/disk trust boundaries on a security regression dependency, covered by defensive-noise's integrity exception.

items.quote: def generate(ids, tables, effect_rows, factions, maps, items, locks):
items.what: generate() spans about 95 lines (224-316) and mixes six jobs: scroll to recipe resolution (225-236), vendor stock (238-249), quest rewards (251-257), spawn/faction filtering via the nested keep() closure that mutates the outer npcs and factionless (259-275), best-source selection per recipe (277-295), then trainers, reagents and the used-NPC pruning (296-316). Proposed split: resolve_scrolls, scroll_sources and a small NPC-placement class or function that owns npcs/factionless.
items.why: Each step feeds the next only through a handful of dicts, so they separate cleanly. The closure with shared mutable state (keep) is why the trainer and reagent pruning must be called in a fixed order after the source loop. Only tests cover gathered(), so generate() itself is unreached by tests. A split belongs in its own reviewed change.
items.reason: The stages share scroll membership, NPC validity and final used-NPC pruning to produce one internally consistent data record, rather than independent unrelated outputs; the synthetic vendor fixture exercises those dependencies. Its roughly 95 lines and shallow staged loops alone do not establish an oversized-module defect.

items.what: gathered() builds its own reference_loot_template index and expansion (lines 148-155, 172-175) beside scroll_drops()'s (lines 255-275) and loot_chances() (236-249), the canonical CMaNGOS loot resolution in the same file.
items.why: Differences look like drift: expand() follows references one level only (nested refs are yielded as rows whose item is the ref row's, not expanded); referenced rows' chances are used unscaled by the referencing row's chance; chance 0 is treated as 'main yield' rather than loot_chances' equal share of the group's remainder. scroll_drops does recursion with a cycle guard and scaling. Output effect on current data not measured; GatheredBy uses a 10% threshold, so unscaled referenced chances could admit items below it.
items.reason: gathered() resolves reference loot through loot_items, shared with scroll_drops, with multiplied chances; regenerated Data/Sources.lua is byte-identical
items.guard: lens-only: a behaviour bug, not a shape a rule can match; regression test tools/gen_sources_test.py

items.what: Resolving which creatures sell an item (npc_vendor rows plus npc_vendor_template expanded through creature_template.VendorTemplateId) is written twice in gen_sources.py: reagent_vendors (lines 200-213) and inline in generate (lines 306-316). Canonical: one helper returning {item: {entry: limited}}; reagent_vendors keeps the entries whose limited flag is False.
items.why: Same three loops over the same tables and the same VendorTemplateId join. Only difference: reagent_vendors filters maxcount == 0 and returns sets; generate keeps maxcount > 0 as a 'limited' flag. That is a filter on the same result, not a different concept; a fix to the template join (e.g. a template entry also listed directly) would need both.
items.reason: owner-delegated 2026-09-27: wontfix, a shared vendor join isn't behaviour-preserving (a direct-unlimited/template-limited seller changes class).

items.quote: REAGENT = re.compile(r"itemID = (\d+), quantity")
items.what: gen_sources re-parses other generators' Lua output with its own regexes (REAGENT against gen_recipes.render, VENDOR_ROW against gen_vendor.render), as gen_recipes.threshold_ids does against gen_thresholds.render. Each output row format therefore lives twice, in the renderer and in a reader in another file.
items.why: REAGENT also matches `output = { itemID = N, quantity = ... }`, so reagent_items() returns recipe outputs too, contrary to its name; checked against current Data: no GatheredBy item is an output-only item, so no effect today. Both use finditer, so a render format change yields fewer items silently rather than an error (threshold_ids by contrast fullmatches every row and raises). Canonical home would be a reader beside each render.
